title: Everything It Can See

post.author: u/projection_box_wilmer
post.title: Our night assistant knows only what's pinned to the inspector's wall. On Monday our clerk pinned everything. At 02:14 it named the man who unlocks the building for us.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer, and three nights a week I volunteer with a cold-case group that meets in the old projection box of the Alcazar, a cinema that closed in 1991. In February 1983 the projectionist, Casimir Ledwith, walked out of this box during the late show and was never seen again. His last reel ran out at 23:58, and the screen stayed white until somebody came up.

Inspector Vossberg, retired, keeps the wall: files, statements and photographs, each typed up as text. In the spring I built the night assistant. With every question my app sends a model the standing instructions and two worked answers as the system prompt, then the cards she has pinned, then tonight's conversation, kept to its last ten turns, then the question. Prompt caching is on, with the cache breakpoint, the marker where the reusable part of a request ends, after the last card. The volunteers ask it something about every three minutes, some 120 calls a night. The app's budget is 60,000 tokens a request.

On Monday Gideon, our new clerk, found a print in the Alcazar's old poster boxes and pinned it. Then, so nothing would ever be missed, he pinned everything else: every file, the clippings, the takings book, September's saved conversation about another case. With the system prompt, both conversations and the question, that's 14 items and 38,300 tokens. It all fit. He also moved the question up, straight after the system prompt, so the assistant would know what to look for before it read.

02:14  question  Who was the last person seen with Casimir Ledwith?
02:14  reply     Emrys Brask, the usher: he took Mr Ledwith a coffee
                 at 23:30 (DS Pennick's notes, 1983).
Mr Brask is 81. He was the usher that night, and he is our caretaker now. He was standing behind me with the tea tray.
He said: I was selling tickets.

Gideon's print is a photograph of the foyer, taken for a poster, the clock at 23:40. Mr Brask is at the ticket kiosk. Through the side door, Casimir is talking to a man in a houndstooth overcoat. On the back, in pencil: C. L. and his brother, side door. In 1983 Fenwick Ledwith told the police he spent that evening at home in Dunmore.

The photograph was on the wall the whole time. And last night's bill was nearly eighteen times a September night's. The inspector wants the assistant back on Thursday. What happened, and what do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glad the tea survived, and nothing in that projection box is haunted. Your assistant is a language model, and on each call it sees only what your app sends. That whole set of tokens is the call's context: system prompt, examples, cards, conversation and question together. Deciding what goes into it, and in what order, is context engineering. Two words for your usage page, too. A cache write is the provider storing its work on everything up to your breakpoint, billed a little above the normal input price. A cache read is reusing that work when a later request matches it exactly, billed at a small fraction. Two questions. On the 02:14 request, where did the foyer photograph sit, and how many of the 38,300 tokens had anything to do with who was with Casimir at 23:40? And on the usage page, what share of a September night's input tokens were cache reads, and what share of last night's?

replies.author: u/projection_box_wilmer
replies.text: Item 9 of 14, tokens 18,400 to 19,000 of 38,300: the middle. The inspector and I sorted the rest this morning. 10,400 tokens bear on that question and 27,900 don't. DS Pennick's 1983 notes are 9,600 of them, and they name Mr Brask 14 times. A review in 1985 set them aside, which is why she never pinned them. On the usage page, 84 percent of a September night's input tokens were cache reads. Last night, none. All 120 calls wrote 30,600 tokens to the cache, and not one read them back.

comments.author: u/contact_sheet_morwenna
comments.text: My father photographed cinema foyers in the eighties, for posters. He pencilled who was in every print on the back, because the managers always asked. Years later he told me about one February night at a cinema with a white screen, where two brothers were arguing at the side door while he set up his lights, and nobody went up to change the reel. He said no one ever came to ask him about it. I still have his contact sheets.

replies.author: u/projection_box_wilmer
replies.text: The inspector asks if you could bring them on Thursday, any time after ten. Mr Brask will let you in.

comments.author: u/runbook_search_kerensa
comments.text: Same thing at work, without the projection box. Our on-call assistant did well with five runbooks, the step-by-step guides for fixing each alarm. Then someone connected the whole wiki, about 600 pages, so it would never miss anything, and the answers got worse. It started quoting a database runbook we retired in 2022, which was longer than the current one and named the alarm more often. Nothing errored. The bill went up too, and it was a month before anyone put the two together.

reply.prompt: The inspector wants the assistant back on Thursday night. What should Wilmer change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Take DS Pennick's notes off the wall, since that's where Mr Brask's name came from, and leave the rest as Gideon built it. Every other card is real evidence, and the assistant should see all of it.
options.verdict: One card down, the noise stays
options.part2: I took DS Pennick's notes down and replayed the 02:14 question. It stopped naming Mr Brask. It said the wall doesn't settle who was last seen with Casimir. The photograph sat near the top now, tokens 8,800 to 9,400 of 28,700, but 18,300 of those tokens still had nothing to do with the question: the clippings, the takings book, September's conversation and two photographs. And the night still cost $8.15, with no cache reads at all: the question still sat above the breakpoint, so every call wrote 21,000 tokens and none read them back.
options.senior: Taking down the one card that misled it treats a symptom. Everything else that doesn't bear on the question still crowds what does, and a question above the breakpoint still makes every call a fresh cache write. Decide what each question needs, not just what to throw out.

options.text: Pin only what each line of inquiry needs; the notes the 1985 review set aside stay in the archive. Keep the standing parts first in a fixed order, the question last, caching on, and test the side-door question.
options.part2: The inspector and I sorted the cards by the questions they answer. For who was with Casimir that night: the instructions and worked answers, the case file, both 1983 statements and the foyer photograph, then tonight's conversation, and the question last. 10,400 tokens. DS Pennick's notes, the clippings and the takings book stay in the archive, where people read them. The photograph now sits near the end, tokens 8,200 to 8,800. At 02:14 on Thursday it answered: Fenwick Ledwith, his brother, side door, 23:40, from the foyer photograph and the pencil note on its back. Mr Brask read it and put the tray down. The night cost $0.62, and 84 percent of input tokens were cache reads again. The side-door question now runs as a test before any change to the wall.
options.senior: Treat the context as a budget. Send the smallest set of cards that answers the question, in a fixed order with the stable parts first and the question last: clearer for the model and cheaper to repeat. Then check that the card that matters arrives, and watch the share read from the cache.

options.text: Keep everything pinned, but have the app re-pin the wall in a new order before every call, so no card stays stuck in the middle and the photograph gets its turn near the top of each request.
options.verdict: A new order every call, nothing reused
options.part2: I had the app re-pin the wall in a new order before every call, the top card to the bottom each time, with the question back at the end, and replayed last night's 120 calls. The photograph moved: it sat near the top on 53 calls, in the middle on 28 and near the end on 39. Asked the 02:14 question at any of them, the assistant named Mr Brask: the 27,900 tokens that had nothing to do with it moved with the photograph. And no call ever read the cache, since no two calls started the same way. The night cost $11.02, more than with caching switched off.
options.senior: Moving the middle around doesn't shrink it. And prompt caching needs the start of each request identical, byte for byte: a prefix that changes every call is written every call and never read, so you pay the write premium for nothing.

options.text: Keep everything pinned, since one missed card is worse than a long request, but move the question back to the end, where it was. Caching starts working again, and the bill drops to a few dollars a night.
options.verdict: Trade-off: the bill, not the answer
options.part2: I moved the question back to the end and left all 14 items in. The night cost $2.67, and 79 percent of input tokens were cache reads. Then I asked the 02:14 question again. The photograph sat at tokens 18,300 to 18,900 of 38,300, still the middle, behind DS Pennick's notes, and the assistant named Mr Brask. Gideon said at least it was cheaper to be wrong.
options.senior: Order fixes the bill: a stable prefix is read from the cache at a tenth of the price. It doesn't fix what the model has to wade through. Caching changes what you pay for tokens, not whether they get in the way.

sim.title: Pin the evidence wall yourself
sim.lede: You're Wilmer at six in the morning with the 02:14 request open. The wall holds 14 cards: the standing instructions and two worked answers, which make the system prompt; nine wall cards of files, statements and photographs; September's saved conversation; tonight's conversation; and the question, always sent. Token counts are teaching values made up for the case, and the sim knows which cards bear on the question, which your app wouldn't. Pick a wall, or press cards to pin and unpin them. Pick the order: Gideon's, with the question straight after the system prompt; the standing parts first and the question last; or re-pinned in a new order every call, the top wall card going to the bottom and the question last. Set the budget per request, the most tokens the app will send, and whether to trim the history to fit it, September's conversation first. A pinned card is never trimmed, so a request that still doesn't fit is not sent. The answer is a teaching rule, not a model: right only when the foyer photograph is in, outside the middle third of the request, and no more than 8,000 tokens are not needed; otherwise Mr Brask if DS Pennick's notes are in, or no name. The night replays the calls three minutes apart, inside the cache's documented five-minute lifetime. The cache breakpoint sits after the last wall card, and a cache read needs everything before it to match the previous call exactly, at least 1,024 tokens of it, one of the documented minimums. Prices are teaching values, $2 per million input tokens, with Anthropic's standard documented multipliers: 1.25 times for a cache write and 0.1 times for a cache read.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on Gideon's 02:14 request: 14 items, 38,300 tokens, the foyer photograph at tokens 18,400 to 19,000, the middle third, 27,900 tokens not needed, and the answer names Mr Brask. The night costs $11.03 with caching and $9.19 without: every call writes the cache and none reads it. Pick standing parts first: $2.67, 79 percent of input tokens read from the cache, and still Mr Brask, the photograph still in the middle. Press DS Pennick's notes off the wall: no name at all, because 18,300 tokens are still not needed. Now pick only what the question needs: 10,400 tokens, the photograph in the last third, Fenwick Ledwith, $0.62 a night. Switch to Gideon's order: the same answer, but every call writes and none reads, $3.03. Pick re-pinned every call: right on 90 of 120 calls, no reads, $3.02. Back on standing parts first, set the budget to 9,000: tonight's conversation is trimmed and the answer holds. At 8,000 nothing is sent.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the projection box is haunted. The assistant knew only what each request carried, and Gideon's carried everything: the foyer photograph sat in the middle of 38,300 tokens, 27,900 of them beside the point and 9,600 of those naming Mr Brask, and the question above the wall meant no call could reuse the last one's work.

steps.title: The model sees only its context: everything sent for one call.
steps.text: Each night the assistant met the wall for the first time. A model keeps nothing between calls, case 9's lesson, so whatever it is to use must arrive in the request. Anthropic's engineering team calls that set of tokens the context, and in 2025 described context engineering as the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference. Prompt engineering, in the same post, is methods for writing and organizing LLM instructions for optimal outcomes. The instructions are one part of the context. The others are the examples, the documents or records, tool results when a model uses tools (case 5 of this season), the conversation history, and the user's current request. Anthropic's context windows page lists what counts: the system prompt, every message, including tool results, images and documents, and your tool definitions. The post calls context engineering iterative: the curation phase happens each time we decide what to pass to the model. Wilmer's app made that decision 120 times a night. On Monday Gideon made it once, for every call: everything.

steps.title: Context is a budget, not a bin.
steps.text: It all fit, which is why nothing warned anyone. Fitting isn't the test. Anthropic's context windows page says more context isn't automatically better: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot (case 5's term), and that makes curating what's in context just as important as how much space is available. The 2025 post explains that LLMs have an attention budget, that every new token introduced depletes this budget by some amount, and that the decline shows up across all models, more gently in some. Its advice is to find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome. Of Gideon's 38,300 tokens, 10,400 bore on the question and 27,900 didn't, and 9,600 of those were DS Pennick's notes, naming Mr Brask 14 times. Nobody can say in advance how much noise a given model tolerates on a given task, so the sim uses a teaching rule: more than 8,000 tokens beside the point and the answer goes wrong. Noise costs money too: every token is input on every call, 120 times a night. And where the photograph sat may have mattered, as the lost-in-the-middle tests in case 9 suggest: in the middle third of a long request, behind the notes.

steps.title: Select what the task needs, then order it: stable first, the question last.
steps.text: Selecting comes first: which cards does this question need? Here the inspector and Wilmer chose by hand, for one line of inquiry. Season 3 builds retrieval, which looks up the relevant records automatically, and the 2025 post describes agents that keep lightweight references and load data just in time with tools. Leaving a card out of the request isn't throwing it away: DS Pennick's notes stay in the archive, where people read them. Then order. The system prompt has its own slot ahead of the messages, so the standing instructions and examples come first anyway. Inside the messages, Anthropic's long-context tips, for inputs of 20k+ tokens, say: Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples. They add that Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs. They also suggest wrapping each document in <document> tags with its source, and asking for the relevant quotes first, which helps Claude focus on the relevant content and ignore the rest of the document. Gideon's reason for putting the question first, so it would know what to look for, sounds right for a person reading a file; Anthropic's tests point the other way. The sim's teaching rule doesn't score where the question sits, only the photograph and the noise. There, the needed cards in this order make 10,400 tokens, the photograph in the last third, and the right name.

steps.title: Prompt caching: keep the stable part identical, and first.
steps.text: A provider can reuse its work on the start of a request it has seen recently. Anthropic's docs describe the steps: the system checks if a prompt prefix, up to a specified cache breakpoint, is already cached from a recent query; if found, it uses the cached version; otherwise it processes the full prompt and caches the prefix once the response begins. The prefix runs through tools, system, and messages (in that order). Cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments, and changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels. By default the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed each time it is used, with a 1-hour option at additional cost, and prompts under a minimum length, 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model, are processed without caching, and no error is returned. Anthropic's pricing page lists the multipliers: a 5-minute cache write at 1.25x base input price, a 1-hour write at 2x, and a cache read at 0.1x base input price, lower still on a few of the newest models. In September Wilmer's wall was the same on every call and the question came after the breakpoint: 84 percent of input tokens were reads. Gideon's question sat above it, so the 30,600 tokens up to the breakpoint were different on every call: written 120 times, read never, $11.03 a night against $9.19 with caching off. The docs warn about exactly this: placing the breakpoint on a block that changes every request writes a fresh entry each time and never hits. Re-pinning every call does the same, $11.02. The usage fields show it: cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens, and if both are 0, the prompt was not cached.

steps.title: Long histories, tool results, and what context can't fix.
steps.text: Conversations grow every turn. Wilmer's app keeps tonight's to its last ten turns and trims history first when a request runs over budget, never a pinned card: case 9's lessons, where a silent trim lost the jetty and a summary can drop the one fact that matters. Anthropic's API also offers server-side compaction, in beta, which summarizes earlier parts of a conversation. Agents make this harder. Each tool result lands in the context too; the 2025 post calls tool result clearing one of the safest lightest touch forms of compaction, and describes structured note-taking outside the window and sub-agents with clean context windows. Case 5 of this season builds tool calling, and Season 4 builds agents. Context also has limits of its own. It can't supply a fact that isn't there: if the volunteer who typed up Gideon's print had left out the pencil note, no selection or order would name Fenwick Ledwith. And it can't make a model stronger than it is: a model too weak for the task, the choice case 8 was about, stays too weak however well its context is chosen.

diagram.aria: How a request is built, every call. Top row: the system prompt, rules and examples, stable and first; the chosen cards, what the task needs, long ones early; the history, trimmed or compacted, changing every call. All three feed the request, in that order, with the question last and everything up to the cache breakpoint reused. Bottom row: the cards left out, stale or unrelated, not sent and kept for people; the request; and measuring it, cache reads and tokens, with the answer checked. Stable parts first, changing parts last.

notes.text: stable parts first, changing parts last
everything up to the breakpoint is reused

explain.caption: Read from the top left. The system prompt comes first in its own slot, then the cards the task needs, long ones early, then the history, trimmed or compacted, and the question last. Everything up to the cache breakpoint stays identical from call to call, so the provider can reuse it. Cards the question doesn't need stay out of the request, kept where people read them. Then measure: cache reads and tokens per call from the usage fields, and a known-answer question that checks the answer.

fix.title: The fix: choose, order, cache, and check
fix.text: Decide what each line of inquiry needs and send only that: here the standing instructions and worked answers, the case file, both 1983 statements and the foyer photograph. Keep what the question doesn't need out of the request but in the archive, where people read it. Put the parts that never change first, in a fixed order, the long cards before the conversation, and the question last. Trim the history to fit the budget, oldest first, and never drop a pinned card silently: if the pinned cards don't fit, refuse and say so. Put the cache breakpoint on the last part that stays identical, and keep anything that changes, the question, a timestamp, a user's name, after it. Then measure: tokens per call, the share of input tokens read from the cache, and a known-answer question, here who was with Casimir at 23:40, that runs before any change to the wall. In the sim that is 10,400 tokens, the right name on all 120 calls, $0.62 a night and 84 percent read from the cache, against Gideon's 38,300 tokens, Mr Brask and $11.03.

limits: Context can't supply what isn't there. If the description of Gideon's print had left out the pencil note, or the print had never been found, no choice or order of cards would name Fenwick Ledwith; and a model too weak for the task stays weak however good its context is. Check the answers, not just the request.

Selection has a cost of its own. Choosing different cards for each question changes what comes before the breakpoint, so less can be reused: keep a stable core first and put the cards picked for each question after it. Cached tokens still count toward the context window, and caching needs a prefix over the model's minimum and calls inside the lifetime: three minutes apart here, inside five.

The sim's rule is a teaching simplification: the 8,000-token limit and the thirds are made up, and real models vary by task and version; the lost-in-the-middle tests measured 2023 models on shorter inputs than this one. Measure on your own model, with known-answer questions placed in long, noisy inputs. Standards readiness: sending a provider only what a task needs is also data minimisation (case 9). Witness statements are personal data, so this matters wherever the GDPR applies, and inside an ISO/IEC 27001 certified scope under Annex A control 5.34. Build it in now, not at audit time.

explain.seniorTake: A model sees only its context, and choosing that context is the job: what goes in, in what order, and what stays out. Treat the window as a budget, not a bin. Send the smallest set that answers the task, stable parts first and the changing request last, so it reads clearly and caches cheaply. Then measure both sides: whether the card that matters arrives and gets used, and how much of each call is read from the cache.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: context engineering, 2025
realWorld.text: On 29 September 2025 Anthropic's Applied AI team published Effective context engineering for AI agents. It defines context as the set of tokens included when sampling from a large-language model, and context engineering as the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference. Prompt engineering, it says, refers to methods for writing and organizing LLM instructions for optimal outcomes; context engineering manages the whole context state, from system instructions and tools to external data and message history. It calls context engineering iterative: the curation phase happens each time we decide what to pass to the model.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a finite attention budget
realWorld.text: The same post says studies on needle-in-a-haystack style benchmarking have uncovered context rot: as the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases. While some models exhibit more gentle degradation than others, this characteristic emerges across all models. LLMs, it says, have an attention budget, and every new token introduced depletes this budget by some amount, so context must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns. Good context engineering means finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome, and it expects that context windows of all sizes will be subject to context pollution and information relevance concerns.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: more context isn't automatically better
realWorld.text: Anthropic's context windows page, with windows of up to 1M tokens, depending on the model, says a larger context window allows the model to handle more complex and lengthy prompts, but more context isn't automatically better. As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. This makes curating what's in context just as important as how much space is available. Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message, including tool results, images and documents, and the tool definitions. And cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window: prompt caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: long documents first, the question last
realWorld.text: Anthropic's prompting best practices page has a section on long context prompting, for large documents or data-rich inputs (20k+ tokens). Put longform data at the top: Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples. This improves performance across all models. Its note: Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs. It suggests wrapping each document in <document> tags with <document_content> and <source> (and other metadata) subtags, and, for long document tasks, asking Claude to quote relevant parts of the documents first: This helps Claude focus on the relevant content and ignore the rest of the document.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: how prompt caching matches
realWorld.text: Anthropic's prompt caching docs say the system checks if a prompt prefix, up to a specified cache breakpoint, is already cached from a recent query, and that prompt caching references the entire prompt: tools, system, and messages (in that order). Cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments, including all text and images up to and including the block marked with cache control, and changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels. The advice: Place static content (tool definitions, system instructions, context, examples) at the beginning of your prompt, and put the breakpoint on the last block that stays identical; placing it on a block that changes every request (such as a timestamp or the user's arbitrary input) writes a fresh entry each time and never hits. By default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed each time the cached content is used and measured from the start of the request; a 1-hour duration costs extra. The minimum cacheable prompt length runs from 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model, and shorter prompts are processed without caching, with no error returned. Caches are isolated between organizations, and on Anthropic's own API between workspaces too.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: what caching costs
realWorld.text: Anthropic's pricing page lists the prompt caching multipliers relative to base input token rates: a 5-minute cache write at 1.25x base input price, a 1-hour cache write at 2x base input price, and a cache read (hit) at 0.1x base input price, with lower read multipliers on a few of the newest models. A cache hit costs 10% of the standard input price, which means caching pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration (1.25x write), or after two cache reads for the 1-hour duration (2x write). The sim uses the standard multipliers on a teaching base price.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: keep the prefix stable
realWorld.text: OpenAI's prompt caching guide says Prompt caching is enabled by default for supported OpenAI models, and that Cache reuse requires the entire rendered prefix to match. Its advice: Keep the prefix stable. Put stable developer instructions and shared reference material first. If developer instructions or shared material contain timestamps, user-specific content, or other dynamic content, place those at the end rather than the beginning, or move them into later conversation messages. Two providers, one rule: what stays the same goes first.

realWorld.title: Lost in the middle, again
realWorld.text: Case 9 met Liu and colleagues' 2023 finding: in long inputs, models tended to use relevant information at the start or end better than information in the middle. Gideon's wall put the photograph in the middle third of 38,300 tokens. The sim's thirds are a teaching rule inspired by that finding, not its measurements.

asked: What is context engineering, and how is it different from prompt engineering?
How do you decide what goes into the context?
How does prompt caching work, and what breaks it?
Your agent's answers got worse as you added more documents. Why?
interview.answer: Context is everything a model is sent for one call: the system prompt, examples, documents or records, tool definitions and tool results, the conversation history and the request. The model knows nothing else, so choosing that set, and its order, is context engineering. Prompt engineering is part of it, writing the instructions well; context engineering decides, on every call, everything else that goes in. To decide what goes in, I start from the task: what does this request need? Standing instructions and a few examples always; then only the records that bear on it, picked by hand for a narrow task or by retrieval for a large store; history trimmed or summarized to what still matters; and nothing stale or unrelated, which I keep where people can read it. Then I order it: stable parts first, long documents before the question, the question last. Prompt caching lets a provider reuse its work on a prefix it has seen recently. On Anthropic's API the prefix runs through tools, system and messages up to a cache breakpoint, a hit needs it 100 percent identical, the default lifetime is five minutes, refreshed on use, and on most models a read costs a tenth of the base input price while a five-minute write costs 1.25 times. Anything that changes the start breaks it: a timestamp at the top, the user's question before the documents, records in a different order, edited tool definitions, or calls further apart than the lifetime. I put the breakpoint on the last stable block and watch cache_read_input_tokens. Answers getting worse as documents are added usually means noise: irrelevant or outdated documents dilute what matters, can mislead outright, push the key one into the middle, and cost tokens on every call. Anthropic calls the decline context rot. I'd measure it with known-answer questions on long inputs, then select fewer and more relevant documents, retrieve per question, and drop or mark the outdated ones.

terms.def: Everything a model is sent for one call: the system prompt, examples, documents, tool results, conversation history and the request. The model knows nothing else.
Choosing what goes into a model's context on each call, and in what order, so the task gets what it needs and little else. Anthropic's 2025 post named it.
Writing and organizing a model's instructions well, as case 2 of this season did. Context engineering includes it and decides everything else that goes in.
A provider storing its processed work on the start of a request, up to the cache breakpoint, for reuse. Anthropic bills a 5-minute write at 1.25 times the base input price.
Reusing stored work because a later request matches it exactly up to the breakpoint. Billed at 0.1 times the base input price on most Anthropic models. Also called a cache hit.
The marker in a request where the reusable part ends. Everything before it must match a recent request exactly for a cache read. On Anthropic's API it is a field set on one block.
One piece of a request's content, such as a passage of text, an image or a tool result. Cache breakpoints are set on blocks.
How long a stored prefix stays reusable. Anthropic's default is 5 minutes, refreshed by every read and counted from the start of the request; a 1-hour option costs more to write.
Counts in a response's usage: cache_creation_input_tokens (written to the cache), cache_read_input_tokens (read from it) and input_tokens (the rest).
The share of calls, or of input tokens, read from the cache. Wilmer's September nights read 84 percent of input tokens. A sudden fall means something early started changing.
A model's normal price for input tokens, before any cache multiplier. Here a teaching value of $2 per million tokens.
Here, the number the base input price is multiplied by for a cache write or read, such as 1.25 or 0.1.
In OpenAI's words, the start of a request as the provider assembles it, its own instructions and tool definitions included, which must match for a cache read.
The most tokens an app will send in one request: its own cap, below the model's context window. Wilmer's is 60,000.
A made-up number, such as each card's token count here, chosen to show the idea. It is not measured from any real model, tokenizer or bill.
The sim's made-up rule for when the assistant answers right. It stands in for a model to show the idea and measures nothing.
Here, tokens in the context that don't bear on the task. They cost money on every call and can crowd out or contradict what matters.
Anthropic's picture of a model's limited capacity to use what's in its context: every token added uses up some of it.
Tokens that bear on the task at hand, as opposed to noise.
Each extra unit helping less than the one before it.
A kind of test that hides one fact in a long input and asks a model to find it.
The 2025 post's name for irrelevant or misleading material building up in a model's context.
To choose carefully what to include and what to leave out, and keep that choice up to date.
One question an investigation is following, such as who was with Casimir at 23:40.
A tool's name, description and input schema, sent with each request so the model knows it can ask for it. It counts as input tokens.
What your code sends back to the model after running a tool the model asked for. It joins the context like any other message. Case 5 of this season covers it.
A model asking your app to run a tool, such as a search, then using what comes back. Case 5 of this season covers it.
Removing old tool results from an agent's context once they have served their purpose. Anthropic's API offers it.
An agent writing notes to storage outside its context window and reading them back later, so a long task doesn't depend on one window.
A helper agent given one focused task with its own clean context window, which reports back a short result.
Here, loading data into the context only when a step needs it, using tools and stored references, instead of sending everything up front.
Information about a document rather than its content, such as its source or its date.
A date and time written into a message or record. At the top of a prompt it changes on every call.
Short for one million, as in a 1M-token context window.
A step-by-step guide for handling one alarm or task, written for whoever is on call.
A website a team edits together to keep its documentation.
Being the person responsible for answering alarms out of hours.
A board where an investigator pins photographs, notes and documents to see a whole case at once.
Here, one item on the wall, typed up as text the app can send: a file, a statement, a photograph described in words, or a saved conversation.
An unsolved case from years ago, reopened by people who hope to close it.
A police rank above sergeant. Inspector Vossberg is retired and keeps the cold-case group's wall.
Detective sergeant, a police rank below inspector. DS Pennick ran the 1983 inquiry.
A witness's account of what they saw, written down and signed.
Where old records are stored and kept for people to consult.
The small room at the back of a cinema where the projectors run.
The person who runs a cinema's projectors and changes the reels.
A spool of film. A feature used to be split over several reels, each changed by hand as the last ran out.
A cinema's last regular screening of the evening.
The entrance hall of a cinema or theatre, where tickets are sold.
The small booth in a cinema foyer where tickets are sold.
A cinema worker who checks tickets and shows people to their seats.
The person who looks after a building, opening it up and locking it at night.
A record of the money a business took in, day by day.
Articles cut from newspapers and kept as a record.
A woollen cloth woven in a broken check of small jagged squares.
A print of every frame on a roll of film at small size, so a photographer can choose which to enlarge.

atWork: Find one prompt your team sends many times a day: a support assistant, a summarizer, an agent. Print the exact request it sends and mark which parts change between calls. Is anything that changes near the top: a timestamp, the user's name, a ticket number, a list that comes back in a different order each time? On Anthropic's API, read cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens over a day of calls. If writes keep coming and reads stay near zero, something early is changing: a timestamp at the very top of a system prompt is enough to make every call a write, and the input bill can grow several times over without an error anywhere. Move what changes after the cache breakpoint, the user's question last, and measure the hit rate again. Then count what goes in: which parts does the task need, and what rides along just in case? Standards-readiness note: sending a provider only what a task needs is also data minimisation wherever the GDPR applies, and falls under ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control 5.34 inside a certified scope. A context that sends every record just in case is the kind of gap an audit finds. Anthropic isolates caches between organizations, and on its API between workspaces, but whatever you send is still processed by the provider, so build the selection in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's research assistant answers analysts' questions from a folder of reports. Last month someone set it to include every report in the folder with every question, 140 of them, so nothing would be missed. The answers have grown vaguer, some cite a report that was withdrawn in the spring, and the monthly bill went up about tenfold. Nothing errors. What's happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: More isn't better: irrelevant and outdated reports dilute what matters, can mislead, and can push the right one into the middle
Select per question: retrieve or pick only the relevant reports, and keep withdrawn ones out
Order it: instructions and stable material first, the question last, with an identical start so prompt caching can reuse it
Measure: tokens per call, the share read from the cache, and known-answer questions that check the right report is used

recall.model: Every question now carries all 140 reports, so the context is mostly noise. The answers get vaguer because the reports that matter are diluted by ones that don't, sometimes buried in the middle of a long input, and the withdrawn report is still in there, so the model can quote it. The bill grows because every one of those tokens is input on every call. I'd select per question: retrieve the few reports relevant to it, or let analysts pick a set, and keep withdrawn reports out of the store the assistant draws from. Then order the request: instructions and any standing material first, the selected reports next, the question last, with the stable start identical across calls so prompt caching can reuse it. Finally I'd measure: tokens per call, the share read from the cache, and a set of known-answer questions that check the right report is found and used, run before and after the change.

recall.prompt: Why did the night assistant name Emrys Brask at 02:14?
options: The foyer photograph wasn't in the request; trimming had dropped it to fit the budget
It was in, but in the middle of 38,300 tokens, behind 9,600 of old notes naming him
The model remembered the 1983 suspicion from old newspapers it was trained on
Prompt caching sent back September's stored answer instead of a fresh one
recall.why: Gideon pinned everything: 38,300 tokens, well under the 60,000 budget, so nothing was trimmed. The foyer photograph was item 9 of 14, tokens 18,400 to 19,000, the middle third, and 27,900 of the tokens didn't bear on the question, DS Pennick's notes naming Mr Brask 14 times among them. A cache stores the provider's work on the start of a request, never an answer, and nothing in the model's training is about the Alcazar.

recall.prompt: A teammate asks what context engineering is, and how it differs from prompt engineering. Answer in plain words.

keyIdeas.idea: Context is everything the model is sent for one call: instructions, examples, documents, tool results, history and the request
Prompt engineering writes the instructions; context engineering chooses and arranges everything that goes in, on every call
It's a budget: more irrelevant material can make answers worse, and every token costs

recall.model: Everything a model is sent for one call is its context: the system prompt, examples, the documents or records, tool results, the conversation so far and the request. The model knows nothing else. Prompt engineering is writing the instructions well. Context engineering is deciding everything that goes in on each call, and in what order: which documents, how much history, what to leave out, what comes first. It treats the context as a budget: irrelevant material can make answers worse and costs tokens on every call, so you aim for the smallest set that does the job.

recall.prompt: A support assistant's system prompt starts with the current time, to the second. Every call sets a cache breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. What happens to prompt caching?
options: Nothing: providers skip timestamps when they compare one prompt with the next
No call reads the cache: the prefix differs in its first line, so every call writes
Only the timestamp is re-read; the rest of the system prompt still comes from the cache
The cache refreshes every minute, so calls within the same minute still read it
recall.why: Anthropic's docs: cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments up to the breakpoint, and placing the breakpoint on a block that changes every request writes a fresh entry each time and never hits. Each write costs 1.25 times the base input price. Move the time after the breakpoint, near the question, and the stable part is read at 0.1 times on most models.

recall.prompt: Anthropic's long-context tips cover a 30,000-token report and one question about it. Which layout do they advise?
options: The question first, so the model knows what to look for as it reads
The report near the top of the prompt, and the question at the end
The report split in two, with the question placed between the halves
The report last, nearest the answer, so its details are freshest
recall.why: For inputs of 20k+ tokens the page says: Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples. It notes that queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs. Gideon put the question first, which also put the changing part ahead of everything that could have been cached.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The side-door question is still answered right; it's one of ten questions with agreed answers that run before any change to the wall. The county has asked us to run the assistant for its five other cold-case groups. Gideon has a plan: one system prompt for everyone that starts with the group's name and today's date, then every card from all six groups' walls, about 900,000 tokens, in every request, because the model's window is a million tokens now and nobody will ever miss a find again.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell Gideon, and what would you build instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Fitting isn't helping: 900,000 tokens mostly beside the point bury what matters and cost on every call, so select per question, for example by retrieval
Shared, stable parts first, and the group's name and the date after the cache breakpoint, so the prefix stays identical and can be read from the cache
Keep each group's records to its own requests: witness statements are personal data, so send only what a question needs
Measure before and after: the ten agreed questions, tokens per call and the cache-read share for each group

coldCase.model: A million-token window means it fits, not that it helps. Six walls in every request is 900,000 tokens, nearly all of it beside any one question: it buries what matters, invites another Mr Brask, and is paid for on every call. I'd keep each group's archive separate and select per question, with retrieval that finds the few cards that bear on it, plus a short standing core. Order matters too: the shared instructions and examples first, identical for every group, and the group's name and the date after the cache breakpoint, near the question, so the prefix stays the same and the cache can be read. A date at the top would make every call a fresh write. Those archives hold witness statements, which are personal data, so each group's requests should carry only its own records and only what the question needs. Then measure before and after: the ten agreed questions for each group, tokens per call, and the share of input read from the cache.

sources.title: Anthropic Applied AI team (Prithvi Rajasekaran, Ethan Dixon, Carly Ryan and Jeremy Hadfield), Effective context engineering for AI agents, Anthropic Engineering, published 29 September 2025, read 7 October 2026: context is the set of tokens included when sampling from a large-language model; context engineering is the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference; prompt engineering refers to methods for writing and organizing LLM instructions for optimal outcomes; the curation phase happens each time we decide what to pass to the model; context rot from needle-in-a-haystack style benchmarking; some models exhibit more gentle degradation than others, but it emerges across all models; an attention budget that every new token depletes; a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns; the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens; context windows of all sizes will be subject to context pollution; just in time context; tool result clearing as one of the safest lightest touch forms of compaction; structured note-taking; sub-agents with clean context windows

Anthropic, Context windows (Claude Platform docs), read 7 October 2026: up to 1M tokens, depending on the model; more context isn't automatically better; as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot; curating what's in context is just as important as how much space is available; everything in the request counts toward the context window, the system prompt, every message including tool results, images and documents, and the tool definitions; cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window; server-side compaction in beta

Anthropic, Prompting best practices (Claude Platform docs), Long context prompting, read 7 October 2026: for large documents or data-rich inputs (20k+ tokens), place long documents and inputs near the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions and examples; queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs; wrap each document in <document> tags with <document_content> and <source> subtags; ask Claude to quote relevant parts of the documents first

Anthropic, Prompt caching (Claude Platform docs), read 7 October 2026: the system checks if a prompt prefix, up to a specified cache breakpoint, is already cached from a recent query; tools, system, and messages (in that order); cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments; changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels; place static content at the beginning; a single breakpoint on the last block that stays identical; a breakpoint on a block that changes every request writes a fresh entry each time and never hits; a 5-minute default lifetime, refreshed each time it is used and measured from the start of the request; a 1-hour duration at additional cost; minimum cacheable prompt length 512 to 4,096 tokens by model, shorter prompts processed without caching and no error returned; usage fields cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens; caches isolated between organizations and, on the Claude API, between workspaces

Anthropic, Pricing (Claude Platform docs), Prompt caching, read 7 October 2026: 5-minute cache write 1.25x base input price; 1-hour cache write 2x base input price; cache read (hit) 0.1x base input price, with lower multipliers on a few of the newest models; a cache hit costs 10% of the standard input price, so caching pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration, or after two for the 1-hour duration

OpenAI, Prompt caching guide (developer docs), read 7 October 2026: prompt caching is enabled by default for supported OpenAI models; cache reuse requires the entire rendered prefix to match; keep the prefix stable, with stable developer instructions and shared reference material first; place timestamps, user-specific content or other dynamic content at the end rather than the beginning, or move them into later conversation messages

Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni and Liang, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv 2307.03172, 2023: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and degrades when it is in the middle (covered in case 9)

Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5(1)(c): personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection, Information security management systems, Requirements: Annex A includes control 5.34, privacy and protection of PII
